notes.title: Concept - Value Capture Across the AI Stack
notes.scope: The layer-cake view of where money accrues in AI: silicon (Nvidia) -> cloud/neoclouds -> foundation-model labs -> application layer -> distribution, and why the profit pool is not where the value is created. IN: the stack model, gross-margin reality per layer, a16z's value-capture thesis, picks-and-shovels, model-layer commoditization, value-creation vs value-capture. OUT: serving cost mechanics (link to 07), per-function case studies (link to 21 AI Impact by Business Function), forward compute-buildout scenarios (link to 24 Bubble or Boom).
key_points: Layer model: silicon (Nvidia) -> cloud/neoclouds -> foundation-model labs -> app layer -> distribution. As of 2026 the clearest profit pool is silicon: Nvidia data-center revenue ~$115B FY2025 at ~75% gross margin (E3, audited 10-K), while the app layer runs 50-60% gross margin (E1, Bessemer/a16z 2026).

a16z 'Who Owns the Generative AI Platform?' (Jan 2023, E1) argued infrastructure captures the most durable value while apps struggle with retention and margins and models sit in between — a thesis largely borne out by 2026.
'Picks and shovels': the surest returns have flowed to compute suppliers (Nvidia, TSMC, CoreWeave) rather than to model or app builders — the buildout enriches the arms dealer first.

The model layer is commoditizing: token price deflation and open-weight parity (DeepSeek, Llama) compress model-layer margins, pushing durable value toward apps with proprietary workflow/data and toward infra.

The 'thin-margin sandwich': app companies buy inference cost-plus from labs who buy GPUs from Nvidia; each layer's pricing power squeezes the next, so app-layer margins are structurally pinched (link Unit Economics, Moats).

Counter-evidence: app-layer breakouts like Cursor ($500M+ ARR by mid-2025, E2) show apps can capture value fast — but usually on the model providers' compute, so top-line speed is not the same as a durable profit pool (link The Cursor Ramp).

Non-obvious: value capture is not value creation — most measured economic value (McKinsey $2.6-4.4T/yr, E1) accrues to AI *users* (enterprises cutting cost), not AI *vendors*, mirroring prior general-purpose-technology waves where suppliers under-captured the surplus.

notes.title: Concept - Token Price Deflation
notes.scope: The rapid, sustained fall in the price of a fixed quality level of LLM inference ('LLMflation') and what it does to AI business models. IN: the ~10x/year deflation rate, GPT-4-class price history, the drivers (hardware, algorithms, open-weight competition), Epoch's per-benchmark variation, Jevons dynamics, business implications. OUT: the serving mechanisms that enable it (link to 07 quantization/batching), scaling-law compute economics (link to 04), forward extrapolation (link to 24).
key_points: a16z 'LLMflation' (Guido Appenzeller, Nov 2024, E1): for a model of fixed quality, inference cost falls roughly 10x per year; a GPT-3-quality token fell ~1000x in ~3 years.

Frontier-quality price history (E3, published price lists): GPT-4 launched Mar 2023 at $30/$60 per million input/output tokens; GPT-4o (2024) $2.50/$10; GPT-4o-mini $0.15/$0.60; GPT-4-class open weights (DeepSeek V3, Llama 3.3 70B) under $0.50/M — a >60x drop at constant quality.
Epoch AI (2025, E2): the deflation rate varies 9x-900x per year depending on which capability milestone you hold fixed — commodity tasks deflate fastest, frontier capability slowest.

Drivers: cheaper hardware ($/FLOP), algorithmic efficiency (distillation, quantization, MoE), and competition/open weights; DeepSeek's Jan 2025 release crystallized the 'cheap frontier' narrative and knocked ~$589B off Nvidia in a day (E3).

Business implication: any margin that depends on today's token price evaporates at next year's price — cost-plus token pricing is a melting ice cube; conversely, inference-heavy features become economical on a predictable delay.

Jevons paradox: Satya Nadella invoked it (Jan 2025, E2) — cheaper tokens expand total usage, so aggregate AI spend can rise even as per-token price collapses (link Unit Economics, Frontier Lab Economics).

Non-obvious: deflation is per-quality-level, not per-token-you-actually-buy — frontier users keep paying top dollar for the newest (more expensive) capability, so labs' revenue grows even as unit prices fall.

notes.title: Concept - Unit Economics of LLM Products
notes.scope: The COGS and gross-margin math of an AI product: what each query actually costs, why AI gross margins (50-60%) trail SaaS (80-90%), and the levers that move them. IN: per-query cost model, variable vs fixed cost, the broken SaaS zero-marginal-cost assumption, margin levers (caching, routing, small models), power-user risk, per-cohort measurement. OUT: serving-engine cost internals (link to 07), LLMOps cost tooling/gateways (link to 16), forward capex (link to 24).
key_points: The SaaS assumption (marginal serving cost ~ 0) breaks: inference is a real per-query variable cost, so AI products run COGS ~40-50% -> gross margins 50-60% vs SaaS 80-90% (E1, Bessemer Feb 2026 and a16z framing); ICONIQ's 2026 survey put model-inference at ~23% of spend and rising with usage (E2, single survey).

Cost drivers per query: input+output tokens (output typically priced 3-5x input), retries and self-consistency sampling, RAG embedding + retrieval calls, and reasoning models' hidden thinking tokens (can 5-20x output volume).

Margin levers: prompt caching (up to ~90% off cached input), semantic caching, model routing/cascades (cheap model first, escalate on failure), quantized/distilled small models, and batching — each trades quality or latency for COGS (link Cost Engineering for LLM Applications 16).

The power-user problem: flat-rate or seat pricing on a token-metered backend makes heavy users gross-margin-negative; unlimited plans invert SaaS economics, which is why coding tools (Cursor, Claude Code) repeatedly repriced in 2025 (E2, reporting).

Deflation cuts both ways: token deflation improves margins over time, but competition passes the savings to customers and agents/reasoning raise token volume per task — net margin is a race, not a gift (link Token Price Deflation, Frontier Lab Economics).
Measure per-feature, per-cohort unit economics (cost per resolved ticket, per generated PR), never blended — one runaway agent workflow can erase the margin of an entire product line.

Non-obvious: gross margin is a moving target set by your *worst* users and your *newest* model choice; teams that don't instrument token cost per request discover their COGS only when the monthly bill arrives (link Measuring AI ROI).

notes.title: Decision - Build vs Buy vs Wrap
notes.scope: The strategic choice among training/owning a model (build), consuming a foundation model via API (buy), or building product/workflow on top of one (wrap): cost thresholds, defensibility, platform risk, and when each wins. IN: the decision axes, cost crossovers, the 'thin wrapper' failure test, platform-risk quantification, the buy-then-selectively-build path. OUT: the fine-tune-vs-RAG-vs-prompt technical choice (link to 12), agent-framework build decisions (link to 10), per-function ROI (link to 21).
key_points: Default (as of 2026): buy or wrap. Pretraining a frontier model costs $100M-$1B+ (E1 estimates, link Frontier Lab Economics) and deflating token prices make owning a model economically irrational for all but labs and a few sovereign/vertical plays.

'Wrap' = build product, workflow, and data on top of a bought model; the pejorative 'thin wrapper' (Jasper — link AI Wrapper Graveyard) applies only when the wrapper adds nothing the model vendor won't ship for free.

Decision axes: differentiation (does the model or you do the hard part?), platform risk (will the lab ship your feature?), data moat, latency/cost/control, compliance/data residency, and volume (self-hosting open weights can beat API only at very high sustained QPS).

Build (train or heavily fine-tune) is justified for proprietary-data verticals, cost at extreme scale, on-prem/regulatory isolation, or a capability the API won't grant — otherwise it is a distraction (link Fine-Tuning vs RAG vs Prompting 12).

The wrapper survival test: own the workflow, the data exhaust, the integrations, and the distribution — not the prompt. Cursor wrapped Anthropic/OpenAI models and still built a ~$9.9B business (E2, TechCrunch 2025) because the IDE workflow and codebase context are the moat (link The Cursor Ramp, Moats).
Platform risk is measurable: ChatGPT's launch (Nov 2022) gutted Jasper a month after its $1.5B round (E2) — build on a vendor and you inherit their roadmap as your competition.

Non-obvious: 'buy' is rarely permanent — the strongest teams start on the best API to find product-market fit, then selectively self-host or fine-tune only the 5% of traffic where unit economics or control demand it (link Unit Economics).

notes.title: Concept - Moats in the AI Application Layer
notes.scope: Where defensibility comes from for AI applications, and why the model itself is not a moat. IN: proprietary data, workflow lock-in, distribution, integration switching cost, network effects, speed as a temporary edge, outcome-data compounding; why 'thin wrapper' fails; commoditization pressure from below. OUT: model-layer/lab moats (link to Frontier Lab Economics), regulatory moats (link to 23 EU AI Act), the wrapper war stories (link to AI Wrapper Graveyard).
key_points: The model is not your moat: capabilities you access via API, competitors access too; token deflation and open weights erase any advantage built purely on 'we use the best model' (link Token Price Deflation).

Durable moats mirror classic software: proprietary/hard-to-get data, deep workflow integration and switching costs, distribution/installed base, and network effects — not prompt cleverness (a16z, Emergence, Greylock 2023-2025 theses, E1).

Data moats are subtler than claimed: generic user prompts aren't defensible, but structured outcome/feedback data tied to a workflow (which fixes users accepted, which resolutions stuck) compounds into eval and fine-tune advantages (link Outcome-Based Pricing, Measuring AI ROI).

Workflow lock-in wins in practice: Cursor's codebase indexing and editor habit, Harvey's legal workflows, and medical scribes' EHR integration (link AI Medical Scribes 21) — the moat is the surrounding system, not the model call.

Platform/wrapper risk quantified: Jasper's $1.5B-to-cut collapse after ChatGPT (link AI Wrapper Graveyard) is the canonical failure; the operative test is 'what happens to us the day the model vendor ships this for free?'

Speed is only a temporary moat: being first with a workflow buys time, not defensibility, and incumbents with distribution (Microsoft/Google embedding AI) can erase a feature-level lead (link Build vs Buy vs Wrap).

Non-obvious: in AI the strongest moat is often being the *system of record* for a workflow's outcomes — whoever captures the labeled result data gets compounding advantages competitors on the same base model cannot copy (link Unit Economics).

notes.title: Reference - AI Market Sizing Claims
notes.scope: A tiered lookup of the big AI market-size, value, and ROI claims with source, date, evidence tier, and the methodological catch on each. IN: McKinsey $2.6-4.4T, PwC $15.7T, Bloomberg gen-AI $1.3T, Sequoia's $600B gap, IDC ROI multipliers, actual lab revenue anchors, and the value/market/spend distinction. OUT: the forecasting track record analysis (link to 24), per-function impact numbers (link to 21 AI Impact by Business Function), bubble scenario (link to 24 Bubble or Boom).
key_points: McKinsey MGI (Jun 2023, E1): gen AI could add $2.6-4.4T *annually* across 63 use cases — a potential-value estimate, not revenue; ~75% concentrates in customer ops, marketing/sales, software engineering, and R&D.

PwC (2017/2023, E1): AI could contribute $15.7T to global GDP by 2030; Bloomberg Intelligence (2023, E1): the generative-AI market reaches ~$1.3T by 2032. These are TAM/GDP models, wildly method-dependent — present as a spread, never averaged into a single figure.

The revenue-reality gap: Sequoia's David Cahn '$600B question' (Sep 2024, E1, updated from his 2023 '$200B' version) — the annual AI revenue needed to justify GPU capex vastly exceeds actual AI revenue (link Circular Financing).

Actual revenue anchors (E2, reporting): OpenAI ~$13B revenue in 2025; Anthropic run-rate in the low-tens-of-billions by 2026 (Epoch AI) — total app-layer revenue is a small fraction of the multi-hundred-billion annual capex.

ROI claims: IDC (Microsoft-commissioned, 2024, E1) 'about $3.70 returned per $1 spent on gen AI' is a vendor-sponsored estimate; contrast MIT NANDA's finding that ~95% of enterprise pilots showed no P&L impact (E2, link Pilot-to-Production Gap 23).

Reading rule: every market-size number here is E1 at best — check who paid for it, whether it measures TAM/GDP/value/revenue, the target year, and whether 'AI' means gen-AI or all AI; those definitions swing figures by 10x.
Core distinction (footnote): 'value/productivity' (economic surplus) != 'market/revenue' (vendor sales) != 'spend/capex' (buyer outlay); most headlines silently conflate all three.

notes.title: Decision - Pricing Models for AI Products
notes.scope: How to choose among seat/subscription, usage/token-metered, credit/hybrid, and outcome-based pricing given variable inference COGS and ongoing token deflation. IN: the four models, margin risk of each, real 2025-2026 repricing moves, why agents break flat pricing, the value-vs-cost decoupling rule. OUT: the deep treatment of outcome pricing (link to Outcome-Based Pricing), COGS mechanics (link to Unit Economics), gateway/metering tooling (link to 16).
key_points: Four models: per-seat (GitHub Copilot ~$19/user/mo), pure usage ($/token API), credit/hybrid (ChatGPT and Cursor tiers plus overage), and outcome-based (Intercom Fin $0.99/resolution — E3, published) — each shifts COGS risk differently.

Seat pricing on a token backend is a trap: a heavy user on a flat seat can be gross-margin-negative; every major coding tool (Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, Replit) repriced or added usage caps in 2025 after power users blew through flat plans (E2, reporting).

Usage pricing aligns cost but repels buyers: unpredictable bills stall enterprise procurement, so hybrid (base subscription + metered overage) became the 2026 default for balancing predictability and margin (E1, Bessemer/OpenView pricing analyses).

Outcome pricing (Sierra, Intercom Fin) is emerging where the outcome is attributable and clearly cheaper than the human it replaces (link Support Deflection Economics 21, Outcome-Based Pricing) — but attribution and gaming are hard.

Deflation forces annual repricing: because token cost falls ~10x/yr (link Token Price Deflation), pricing locked to today's cost either bleeds margin (if priced under) or gets undercut (if priced over) within a year.

Agent and reasoning workloads break flat pricing hardest: one autonomous task can consume 10-100x a chat's tokens, so agent products trend toward usage or outcome pricing (link Agentic Coding in Production 20).

Non-obvious: price on value/outcome, meter on cost — the winning structure decouples what the customer pays for (a resolved ticket, a merged PR) from your token bill, so deflation flows into your margin rather than the customer's (link Unit Economics).

notes.title: Playbook - Measuring AI ROI
notes.scope: An end-to-end procedure to measure the actual return of an AI deployment and avoid the vanity metrics that make most claimed ROI unfalsifiable. IN: baselining, fully-loaded cost, counterfactual attribution, Goodhart-resistant outcome metrics, the quality/liability tail, benchmark sanity-checks, quarterly recomputation. OUT: pilot-to-production organizational blockers (link to 23), per-function benchmark outcomes (link to 21), forecasting (link to 24).
key_points: Step 1 — baseline before deploy: measure the human/legacy process cost and quality first; without a pre-AI baseline any post-hoc ROI is unfalsifiable, the #1 reason claimed 'ROI' is E0 (link Pilot-to-Production Gap 23).

Step 2 — fully-loaded cost: count inference tokens and retries, but also build/integration, prompt/eval maintenance, human oversight/review, and error-remediation — the hidden denominator that turns positive pilots negative (link Unit Economics).

Step 3 — attribution via counterfactual: use an A/B or holdout, not before/after (which confounds seasonality and other changes); METR's 2025 RCT found experienced devs were ~19% *slower* with AI while *believing* they were ~20% faster (E3) — self-reported productivity is unreliable (link METR Developer Slowdown RCT 20).
Step 4 — pick outcome metrics that survive Goodhart: resolved-and-stayed-resolved tickets, merged-and-not-reverted PRs — not 'messages sent' or 'suggestions accepted' (link The Evaluation Gap 23).

Step 5 — subtract the quality/liability tail: deflection that raises churn, AI code that raises defect/rework rates, and hallucination liability (link Hallucination Liability Incidents 23) all net against gross savings.

Sanity-check against the public spread: IDC/Microsoft '$3.70 per $1' (E1, vendor-sponsored) vs MIT NANDA '~95% of pilots, no P&L impact' (E2) — the gap is the point; the honest number is your own measured one.
Verification: recompute ROI on real production data quarterly with updated token prices (deflation helps) and updated usage (agents hurt) — a pilot ROI rarely survives contact with scale.

notes.title: Breakdown - Frontier Lab Economics
notes.scope: The revenue, burn, and capex reality of the frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI): the loss-making growth model, cost structure, revenue mix, capital raised, and compute commitments that dwarf revenue. IN: revenue/ARR figures, burn and path-to-profit, training vs inference COGS, enterprise-vs-consumer mix, mega-raises, the capex-revenue gap. OUT: forward compute-buildout/power scenarios (link to 24), the circular-financing structure (link to Circular Financing), scaling-law compute mechanics (link to 04).
key_points: Revenue (E2, reporting): OpenAI ~$13B revenue in 2025 (up from ~$3.7B in 2024), ~$20B ARR entering 2026; Anthropic scaled from ~$1B ARR at end-2024 to a low-tens-of-billions run-rate by 2026, reportedly overtaking OpenAI's run-rate mid-2026 per Epoch AI.

Burn: OpenAI reportedly lost billions on ~$13B revenue and guides to continued multi-billion losses through the late 2020s, targeting profitability only ~2029-2030 (E2, reporting/company guidance) — growth is funded by capital, not cash flow.

Cost structure: compute dominates. Inference for free consumer users (hundreds of millions of ChatGPT users) is a massive COGS line, and each model generation raises training cost — frontier runs $100M-$1B+ (E1 estimates).

Revenue mix is diverging: Anthropic skews API/enterprise and coding (Claude Code), higher-margin; OpenAI skews consumer subscriptions — two genuinely different business models (E2, Forbes 2026 framing).

Capital raised is unprecedented: OpenAI's $40B round (Mar 2025, SoftBank-led) at ~$300B post was the largest private tech raise ever; Anthropic raised $13B at $183B (Sept 2025) — funding the burn (link Venture Funding Patterns).

Compute commitments exceed revenue by an order of magnitude: OpenAI signed hundreds of billions in Oracle/Nvidia/AMD/Broadcom compute deals against ~$13B revenue — that gap is the entire controversy (link Circular Financing, Bubble or Boom 24).

The Jevons bet: labs wager that cheaper tokens (link Token Price Deflation) expand usage faster than price falls, growing revenue despite deflation — plausible but unproven at the committed capex scale.

Non-obvious / what's dated: 'ARR' for these labs blends volatile consumer subscriptions and capacity-constrained API; press run-rate figures are E2 and move monthly — treat any single number as a snapshot, not audited truth.

notes.title: Breakdown - The Cursor Ramp
notes.scope: Anysphere/Cursor as the fastest application-layer revenue ramp on record and a live case study in wrapper economics: what its numbers reveal about moats (workflow/context), COGS (third-party inference), pricing (repricings), and platform risk. IN: the revenue/valuation ramp, enterprise mix shift, the moat, the margin squeeze, platform risk, transferable lessons. OUT: agentic-coding mechanics (link to Agentic Coding in Production 20), coding-productivity evidence (link to 20), model-provider economics (link to Frontier Lab Economics).
key_points: Ramp (E2, TechCrunch/reporting): Cursor hit ~$100M ARR by Jan 2025 (~2 years from launch) and $500M+ ARR with a $9.9B valuation by June 2025 — among the fastest application-layer revenue ramps ever recorded.

Enterprise shift: revenue moved from individual-developer subscriptions toward enterprise seats through 2025-2026 (E2) — the classic PLG-to-enterprise motion, where durability comes from org-level lock-in rather than the model.

The moat is workflow + context, not the model: Cursor runs on Anthropic/OpenAI frontier models any competitor can call; defensibility is codebase indexing, editor habit, and integrations (link Moats, Build vs Buy vs Wrap).

COGS reality: as a wrapper on third-party inference, Cursor's gross margin is squeezed between subscription revenue and model-API bills — it repriced and added usage limits in 2025 when heavy agent use blew past flat plans (E2, link Pricing Models, Unit Economics).

Platform risk is live: it sells on top of Anthropic while Anthropic ships Claude Code, and OpenAI pursued a rival in the Windsurf saga (2025) — the model vendor is simultaneously supplier and competitor (link AI Wrapper Graveyard).

What to steal: pick a high-frequency professional workflow, own the context/data layer around the model, and convert PLG love into enterprise contracts before the base-model vendor commoditizes the feature.

Non-obvious: Cursor is both the counterexample to 'wrappers can't win' AND proof that 'wrapper margins are structurally thin' — a fast top line on someone else's compute is not the same as a durable profit pool (link Value Capture).

notes.title: Reference - AI Venture Funding Patterns
notes.scope: A lookup of the AI funding landscape: mega-rounds, valuations, VC concentration, revenue multiples, strategic/vendor money, and secondaries. IN: the biggest raises and valuations, the 'AI is most of VC' stat, forward-multiple norms, how strategic compute money blurs 'funding', tender/secondary dynamics, the reading rules. OUT: circular vendor-financing analysis (link to Circular Financing), bubble scenario (link to 24), lab burn detail (link to Frontier Lab Economics).
key_points: Mega-rounds (E2, reporting): OpenAI $40B at ~$300B post (Mar 2025, SoftBank-led), the largest private tech raise in history; Anthropic $3.5B at $61.5B (Mar 2025) then $13B at $183B (Sept 2025); xAI multi-billion raises at ~$50B+ — valuations set as much by strategic/compute partners as by VCs.

Concentration: AI captured the majority of US VC dollars in 2025 (E1/E2, PitchBook/CB Insights), with a handful of foundation-model labs absorbing most of it — simultaneously starving and inflating the rest of the market.
Revenue multiples: labs priced at ~10-30x forward run-rate (E1) — richer than SaaS norms, justified by growth rate and winner-take-most bets rather than profitability (link Frontier Lab Economics).

Strategic/vendor money blurs the line: Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google invest in the same labs that buy their compute (link Circular Financing) — some 'funding' is effectively pre-purchased GPU capacity.
Secondaries and tenders: employee tender offers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Anysphere) convert paper value to cash without an IPO — a marker of a private-market-heavy, IPO-light cycle (E2).
Reading rule: a private 'valuation' is the price of the last (often strategic, structured) share, not a market-clearing price — treat lab valuations as E1 signals, not audited worth.

Footnote: 'raised' != 'revenue' != 'valuation'; and because much 2025-26 capital is earmarked for compute, a raise is often a spending commitment routed straight to the infra layer (link Value Capture).

notes.title: Concept - GPU Depreciation and Compute Capex Accounting
notes.scope: How hyperscalers and neoclouds account for GPU capex, why depreciation-schedule choices swing reported AI profits, and the live debate over whether those schedules overstate earnings. IN: the depreciation mechanism, 4-to-6-year extensions, Burry's critique and the counter, the waterfall model, GPU-backed debt, detection signals. OUT: forward capex/power buildout scenarios (link to 24), the circular-financing structure (link to Circular Financing), GPU hardware internals (link to 08).
key_points: The mechanism: GPUs are capitalized and depreciated over an assumed useful life; lengthening that life lowers annual depreciation and raises reported profit. Microsoft moved server/GPU depreciation from ~4 to 6 years and Meta to ~5.5 years (E2, 10-K disclosures).

Burry's critique (Nov 2025, E2, his own estimate): frontier GPUs economically obsolesce in ~2-3 years (Nvidia's annual Hopper->Blackwell->Rubin cadence), so 5-6yr schedules understate depreciation by ~$176B across the industry 2026-2028, inflating AI-era earnings.

The counter (E1): the 'waterfall' — chips age out of frontier *training* in 18-36 months but keep earning on cheaper inference and older workloads for years, so a long book life is not fraud if the asset genuinely earns over it.

Why it matters economically: depreciation is the single largest cost of the AI buildout; if understated, hyperscaler AI margins and the entire capex-justification math are rosier than reality (link Market Sizing Claims, Circular Financing).
Neocloud leverage: GPU-backed debt financing (CoreWeave et al.) assumes multi-year GPU cash flows to service loans — shorten the real useful life and the debt-coverage math breaks (E2).

Detection signal: watch for depreciation-schedule changes disclosed in 10-Ks around capex ramps, and the widening gap between capex outflow and reported operating income (link Frontier Lab Economics).

Non-obvious: the same physical GPU can be an appreciating scarce asset (during shortage) and a rapidly depreciating one (once the next gen ships and supply loosens) — the accounting picks one story while reality is regime-dependent, and the bull/bear case hinges on which regime holds (link Bubble or Boom 24).

notes.title: Deep Dive - Circular Financing in the AI Buildout
notes.scope: The interlocking money loops of the 2025-2026 AI buildout and the debate over whether they are prudent infrastructure capex or demand manufactured by vendor financing. IN: the Nvidia-OpenAI-Oracle-CoreWeave loops, Stargate, vendor-financing analogy to the telecom bust, the $600B gap, systemic concentration risk, the depreciation tie-in, and the one number that settles it. OUT: bubble scenario/probabilities (link to 24 Bubble or Boom), depreciation accounting (link to GPU Depreciation), scaling-law compute demand (link to 04).
key_points: The pattern: Nvidia committed to invest up to ~$100B in OpenAI (Sept 2025 announcement, E2) while OpenAI commits hundreds of billions to buy Nvidia-powered compute via Oracle, CoreWeave, and Microsoft — capital and chips loop among the same few balance sheets.

More loops: Nvidia is both supplier to and investor in CoreWeave; the OpenAI-Oracle ~$300B compute deal and Project Stargate ($500B, $100B initial, announced Jan 2025) route capital from labs to clouds to Nvidia (E2, announcements — actual spend unverified).

The bear read: vendor financing can inflate demand — a supplier funding its customer's purchases manufactures revenue that isn't end-demand; the analogy is Lucent/Nortel telecom vendor financing before the 2001 bust (E1, analyst analogy).

The bull read: this is how capital-intensive infrastructure has always been built (railroads, telecom, cloud) — strategic investment de-risks buildout ahead of demand, and circular does not mean fraudulent (E1).

The gap that drives the debate: Sequoia's Cahn '$600B question' (E1) — committed capex implies AI revenue that dwarfs today's tens-of-billions of actual lab revenue (link Frontier Lab Economics, Market Sizing Claims).

Systemic risk is concentration: Nvidia, a few labs, and 3-4 hyperscalers are cross-exposed, so a demand shortfall or a DeepSeek-style efficiency shock (Nvidia -$589B in a single day, Jan 2025, E3) transmits across all of them at once.
Depreciation tie-in: the loops assume multi-year GPU cash flows to service GPU-backed debt; if useful life is shorter than booked (link GPU Depreciation), the financing math tightens fast.

Non-obvious: whether it is 'circular financing' or 'ordinary capex' cannot be read off the deal structure — it depends entirely on whether real end-user demand shows up to consume the compute; the identical transactions are prudent or a bubble depending on a number nobody yet has (link Bubble or Boom 24).

notes.title: Concept - Outcome-Based Pricing
notes.scope: Pricing AI by delivered result (per resolution, per successful task) instead of per seat or token, and why agents make it newly possible and newly hard. IN: the definition, real deployments, why agents enable it, the attribution/verification problem, margin alignment under deflation, gaming/adverse selection, where it fails. OUT: the general pricing decision (link to Pricing Models), support-deflection unit math (link to 21 Support Deflection Economics), agent mechanics (link to 10).
key_points: Definition: charge per verified outcome (resolved ticket, booked meeting, merged PR), not per seat or token — the vendor absorbs token COGS and bears delivery risk (link Unit Economics).

Real pricing (E2/E3, published): Intercom Fin $0.99 per resolution; Sierra outcome-based with per-contract undisclosed rates; Salesforce Agentforce launched around $2/conversation before shifting toward flexible/credit models — the market is actively experimenting.

Why now: agents can complete whole tasks autonomously, so the sellable unit becomes the outcome (a labor substitute) rather than a tool — reframing AI as 'selling work' priced against the human it replaces (link Support Deflection Economics 21, Agentic Coding in Production 20).

The attribution problem: you must define and verify the outcome and prove the agent (not a human, not luck) caused it — disputes over what counts as a 'resolution' are the central commercial friction (link The Evaluation Gap 23).

Margin alignment: outcome pricing decouples price (value) from cost (tokens), so token deflation accrues to vendor margin — the structurally best model in a deflationary world (link Token Price Deflation, Pricing Models).

Gaming and adverse selection: customers route only hard cases to a per-outcome agent, and agents can be tuned to over-declare weak 'resolutions' — both sides optimize the metric, so Goodhart-resistant outcome definitions are essential.

Non-obvious: outcome pricing only works where the outcome is cheap to verify and clearly cheaper than the human alternative; where verification is costly or quality is contested (legal, medical advice, liability — link Hallucination Liability Incidents 23), seat/usage pricing persists.

notes.title: Lore - AI Wrapper Graveyard
notes.scope: War stories of application-layer companies erased or maimed by platform shifts, and the folklore of the 'thin wrapper' — plus what the survivors did differently. IN: Jasper vs ChatGPT, the 'GPT-4 killed my startup' wave, the Windsurf saga, the $20/month ceiling, the survivor pattern, honest evidence status. OUT: moats theory (link to Moats), the build/buy/wrap decision (link to Build vs Buy vs Wrap), enterprise-adoption blockers (link to 23).
key_points: Jasper (E2, reporting): raised $125M at a $1.5B valuation in Oct 2022; ChatGPT launched Nov 30, 2022; Jasper later cut its internal valuation and revenue reportedly fell from a ~$120M peak — the canonical 'thin wrapper' cautionary tale.

OpenAI's demo-ware effect: successive releases (GPTs, structured output, code interpreter, Sora) vaporized whole categories of wrappers ('PDF chat', 'AI writer') overnight — folklore-but-real: never build a company on a feature the platform will ship for free.

Windsurf saga (2025, E2): a reported OpenAI acquisition of the coding startup collapsed, Google 'reverse-acquihired' the leadership and licensed the tech, and Cognition acquired the remainder — a live lesson that even successful coding wrappers are pawns in the labs' consolidation.
Survivor pattern: the ones that lived (Cursor, Harvey, Perplexity) owned a workflow, proprietary data/context, or distribution — not a prompt (link Moats, The Cursor Ramp).

The '$20/month ceiling': consumer wrappers competing with ChatGPT's $20 tier lost all pricing power once the base product absorbed their use case — pricing power requires a moat the base model lacks (link Pricing Models).

Evidence status: the Jasper valuation cut and the Windsurf saga are well-reported (E2); specific revenue figures and 'killed by GPT-X' attributions are often founder/press narrative (E1) — directionally true, numerically soft.

The durable lesson operators repeat: 'don't build a business in the model's roadmap' — assume every capability you wrap will be commoditized, and ask what you still own when it is (link Build vs Buy vs Wrap, Value Capture).
